newsitem.title: USA: Biotech pioneer Swanson retiring from Genentech.
newsitem.headline: Biotech pioneer Swanson retiring from Genentech.

text.p: Robert Swanson, a pioneer in the biotechnology industry, will retire as chairman of Genentech Inc., which he co-founded 20 years ago, to devote more time to funding young companies, Genentech said Thursday.
Swanson, 49, will continue as an adviser and consultant to Genentech, one of the nation's leading biotechnology companies, which plans to name a successor at the end of this week.

Genentech said Swanson decided to leave to allow him more time to identify and fund novel young companies, companies much like Genentech was when Swanson launched it with Herbert Boyer, a biochemist, in 1976.

"Bob Swanson's contributions to Genentech cannot be overstated. He launched the biotechnology industry and then successfully helped guide Genentech into a billion dollar company," Genentech Chief Executive Officer Arthur Levinson said in a statement.

Under Swanson's stewardship, Genentech developed 10 important drugs and now markets five of them in the United States, including Activase, a clot buster used in treating heart attacks and strokes, the growth hormone Nutropin and Pulmozyme for cystic fibrosis.
Humulin, which it developed in the 1970s for treating diabetes, is marketed under license by Eli Lilly and Co.

Swanson's decision to leave comes 17 months after the company's board ousted former Genentech Chief Executive Officer G. Kirk Raab after a series of disputes. At the time, the board named Levinson to succeed Raab as CEO.

Raab stepped down after the board voted to seek his resignation following allegations that he sought a $2 million personal loan guarantee from Roche Holding Ltd., the Swiss drug company that owns about two-thirds of Genentech stock and has an option to buy the rest.

Raab had been named to succeed Swanson as CEO in February 1990, when Swanson became chairman. Swanson had been CEO and a director since founding the company with Boyer, who was a biochemist at the University of California at San Francisco.

"My change in role will give me additional time to focus on my first love, venture capital," said Swanson. "It is challenging and exciting to work with bright, creative entrepreneurs whose ideas can change the world, and I look forward to helping them build significant companies."
Swanson will also retire as a director of South San Francisco-based Genentech.

As a 29-year-old venture capitalist, Swanson approached Boyer about the possibility of developing and marketing drugs using technology working with DNA, the genetic material that is the blueprint for human growth.

Before forming Genentech, Swanson was a partner with Kleiner & Perkins, a venture capital partnership in San Francisco, and from 1970 to 1974 he was an investment officer with Citicorp Venture Capital Ltd.
Genentech stock fell 12.5 cents to $53.25 on the New York Stock Exchange in midday trading.
